nameStory: The red-seeded dandelion gets its name from the distinctive reddish color of its seeds, which sets it apart from its yellow-seeded cousin, the common dandelion. While most people never look closely enough at dandelion seeds to notice this difference, botanists use this colorful detail as a key identifying feature. The name is refreshingly straightforward – sometimes plants are named exactly for what makes them unique!
description: Red-seeded dandelion is a low-growing perennial herb that looks remarkably similar to the common dandelion most people know from their lawns. It produces the same familiar yellow flower heads on hollow stems and forms rosettes of deeply lobed leaves that hug the ground. Like other dandelions, it typically grows 4-12 inches tall and develops the classic white, fluffy seed heads that children love to blow. This species is native to Europe but has made itself at home across northern North America.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The seeds (technically fruits) have a distinctive reddish-brown to dark red color when mature, unlike the pale yellow or tan seeds of common dandelion. Look closely at the seed heads when they're fresh – the color difference is most obvious before they dry out completely.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower heads composed of many small ray petals, identical to common dandelion. The flowers are about 1-2 inches across and sit atop hollow, smooth stems that feel slightly rubbery when squeezed and may exude a milky white sap.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves arranged in a ground-hugging rosette, with the classic dandelion 'tooth' shape (the name comes from French 'dent de lion' meaning lion's tooth). Leaves feel somewhat thick and fleshy, with a slightly bitter smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low rosettes that spread close to the ground, with flower stalks rising 4-12 inches high. The entire plant grows from a deep taproot that can extend several inches into the soil.

habitat: Red-seeded dandelion thrives in disturbed soils, roadsides, lawns, fields, and waste areas throughout New England. It prefers full sun to partial shade and adapts well to various soil types, though it's often found in slightly more compacted or disturbed soils than some of its relatives. This hardy species is commonly found in urban and suburban environments where it can take advantage of human-disturbed landscapes.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early and flower buds begin forming. Peak blooming period starts in late spring, with bright yellow flowers opening on sunny days and closing at night or in cloudy weather.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming throughout summer, with plants producing multiple flower heads. Seeds ripen and develop their characteristic red color during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Late-season flowers may still appear, and seed dispersal continues. Leaves remain green and may continue growing until hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Leaves die back to ground level, but the plant survives underground via its deep taproot, ready to emerge again in spring.

funFact: Red-seeded dandelion seeds can travel over 60 miles on their feathery parachutes when caught in strong wind currents, making them some of nature's most accomplished long-distance travelers – and explaining how this European native managed to colonize most of northern North America in just a few centuries!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common dandelion, but the red seeds are the giveaway – common dandelion seeds are pale yellow to tan. Memory trick: 'Red-seeded dandelion has RED seeds' – check the fluffy seed heads when they're fresh for the clearest color difference.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize there are multiple dandelion species, assuming all dandelions are the same plant. Red-seeded dandelion is actually quite common but often overlooked because it requires close examination of the seeds to distinguish it from its more famous relative. Both species are equally edible and have similar uses in folk medicine.
compareHints: Red-seeded dandelion is most easily distinguished from common dandelion by its reddish seeds rather than pale yellow ones. Compared to fen dandelion, it grows in drier, more disturbed habitats rather than wetlands. Unlike cinnamon-fruited dandelion, which has brownish seeds, red-seeded dandelion's seeds are distinctly reddish when fresh and mature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common dandelion is much more widespread than its relatives in New England.
Fen dandelion differs from common dandelion primarily in its exclusive wetland habitat and potentially smaller, more delicate features.
Among New England dandelions, only the cinnamon-fruited dandelion has distinctly brown seeds - common dandelion and red-seeded dandelion both have much paler, straw-colored to light brown fruits.
